content: A growing number of individuals with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are receiving treatment. To enhance diagnostic capabilities, several platforms and assays are being developed to be portable, user-friendly, and suitable for use at the primary point of care. These tests aim to deliver rapid results with accuracy comparable to laboratory-based nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). These considerations were discussed during the STI Guideline Development Group meeting to establish acceptable performance standards for point-of-care tests. Such advancements are expected to improve treatment protocols and reduce the negative consequences of untreated STIs. Rapid diagnostic tests for syphilis are available and typically use whole blood, plasma, or serum, providing results within 5 to 30 minutes. A meta-analysis has shown that these tests have a sensitivity ranging from 75% to 99% and specificity from 92% to 99% when compared to Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA) and Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) tests. Dual rapid diagnostic tests for HIV and syphilis have also been developed, offering high sensitivity and specificity. These tests are cost-effective, provide quick results, and require only a single finger prick, making them a practical option for increasing syphilis testing. Diagnostic tests for both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals with STIs include traditional rapid tests such as microscopy (e.g., Gram stain, wet mount, and dark field), pH strip tests, the Whiff test using potassium hydroxide, and the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test for syphilis. The utility of these tests was extensively discussed during the STI Guideline Development Group meeting and evaluated through modeling exercises. Microscopy, for instance, plays a significant role in diagnosing STIs and other reproductive tract infections. Light microscopy, which uses visible light to illuminate specimens, is commonly employed for identifying microorganisms. It is particularly useful for detecting intracellular gram-negative diplococci in polymorphonuclear leukocytes for the presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea. It is also used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis by identifying an abundance of gram-positive and gram-negative cocci with reduced gram-positive lactobacilli in vaginal flora. Wet-mount microscopy can identify motile trichomonads, confirming a diagnosis of trichomoniasis. Fluorescence microscopy, which operates on the principle of fluorescence, can visualize certain bacteria and viruses not easily seen with light microscopy. This method is used in STI detection to identify pathogens such as Treponema pallidum, Chlamydia trachomatis, and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Dark-field microscopy, another specialized technique, is used to detect Treponema pallidum but requires skilled personnel to differentiate it from non-pathogenic treponemes and other spiral organisms. However, dark-field microscopy is not recommended for oral samples due to the presence of non-pathogenic spirochetes in the oral cavity. Microscopy provides a simple, rapid, and cost-effective diagnostic tool that can be used near the patient, such as in primary healthcare facilities. WHO has developed tools to assist laboratories in implementing quality management systems. Laboratories should also strive to minimize the time between sample collection and result delivery, ideally providing results on the same day. Indicators reflecting the quality of results and rapid turnaround times should be established. These protocols also facilitate training, supervision, and procurement of medicines while reducing the risk of antimicrobial resistance. National guidelines for STI management should be developed in consultation with local STI and public health experts and laboratorians. Flow charts are valuable tools for guiding healthcare providers through the decision-making and treatment process for STIs. These charts typically include an entry point (the presenting symptom), decision points (yes/no questions), and action steps (e.g., treatment, counseling, or referral). Standardized symbols, such as rectangles for actions and diamonds for decisions, help communicate the process clearly. Flow charts are particularly useful for managing syndromic approaches to STI treatment, ensuring that patients receive appropriate care even in resource-limited settings. For urethral discharge syndrome, which is commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, or Trichomonas vaginalis, molecular testing such as NAAT is the gold standard for diagnosis. First-catch urine or urethral swabs are suitable specimens for NAAT. In cases where molecular testing is unavailable, syndromic management is recommended, treating for both gonorrhea and chlamydia. Persistent or recurrent urethral discharge should prompt further testing for antimicrobial resistance and additional pathogens like Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas vaginalis. For vaginal discharge, the most common causes are bacterial vaginosis, Trichomonas vaginalis, and Candida albicans. Infections of the endocervix, such as those caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, may not present with vaginal discharge but can cause mucopurulent discharge or inflammation of the cervical os. Healthcare providers must carefully evaluate the cause of vaginal discharge, considering both infectious and non-infectious etiologies. The recommendations provided in these guidelines aim to assist in the effective management of abnormal vaginal discharge symptoms.
